title: The Autistic Navigator: A CBT Toolkit for Thriving
summary: A seven-module CBT journey designed specifically for the autistic mind. Learn to decode social patterns, build predictability, manage sensory needs, develop emotional literacy, and leverage your special interests—all while honoring your unique way of processing the world.

modules.title: Module 1 • Understanding Your Autistic Brain & Setting Your Course
modules.overview: Welcome to the start of your journey. This foundational module is about building a solid base of self-knowledge. Before we can build strategies for navigating the world, we must first understand the unique and powerful architecture of the mind we're working with. We'll shift the perspective from seeing autism as a set of deficits to understanding it as a different, valid way of processing and experiencing life. We'll set the stage for the practical, skill-building work to come by establishing a framework of acceptance and clear, meaningful goals. Your brain runs on a distinct and powerful operating system. This autistic operating system has incredible strengths—an eye for detail, a capacity for deep focus, a strong sense of logic and justice, and an ability to see patterns others miss. The goal of this program is not to try to rewrite your core operating system. Instead, the goal is to provide you with a user manual—a set of tools, translation guides, and strategies that allow your system to function effectively and thrive in a world that wasn't built with its specifications in mind.
takeaways: You are not defective, you are different. Your brain runs on a distinct and powerful operating system.
CBT for autism uses the S-T-E-S-B Cycle: Situation, Thought, Emotion, Sensation, Behavior.
Understanding your sensory profile, information processing style, and special interests is foundational to building effective strategies.
Self-compassion is the antidote to a lifetime of external criticism. True progress is built on self-acceptance, not self-criticism.
exercises: Create an initial profile snapshot: jot down one sensory sensitivity, one sensory joy, and one special interest that brings you into a state of focus.
Write your why: two sentences on why you chose this program right now and what you hope to gain.
Reframe one external expectation into an authentic, skill-based goal that focuses on reducing distress and increasing your capacity for joy.
homework: My Autistic Profile: Create two columns—'Hypersensitive (Avoid)' and 'Hyposensitive (Seek)'. List at least 3–5 specific sensory experiences for each category across different senses.

Information Processing: Describe one situation where your literal interpretation led to a misunderstanding and what you learned. Describe one situation where your attention to detail was a major advantage.
Special Interests: List 2–3 of your most significant special interests. For each one, write a sentence about why it is important to you.
Refining Your Goals: Write 1–3 meaningful goals for yourself for this program, focusing on reducing distress or improving well-being, not just on 'fitting in.'
Self-Compassion Pledge: Write a short, personal self-compassion statement you can read to yourself when feeling overwhelmed or being self-critical.

modules.title: Module 2 • Building Predictability and Emotional Regulation
modules.overview: Having built a foundation of self-understanding, we now begin constructing the core framework for well-being: a stable and predictable environment, both externally and internally. The autistic brain thrives on order and expends a tremendous amount of energy processing a chaotic and sensorially overwhelming world. Routines are not prisons; they are anchors in a chaotic sea. They reduce anxiety by making the immediate future predictable, prevent decision fatigue by automating small decisions, and provide comfort through repetition and predictability. Autistic burnout is a state of profound physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion. The Spoon Theory helps us manage energy: imagine you wake up each day with a limited number of spoons, and every action costs a certain number. Being a good energy accountant means knowing the cost, budgeting your spoons, and finding ways to recharge. A sensory diet is a carefully planned schedule of sensory activities designed to keep your nervous system regulated throughout the day. Instead of waiting to become overwhelmed, you can proactively provide your brain with the inputs it needs to stay calm and focused. Emotional literacy can be challenging for many autistic individuals (alexithymia). Start with the body—notice raw physical sensations, then use tools like an emotion wheel to translate these sensations into emotional language.
takeaways: Routines are anchors in a chaotic sea—they free up cognitive resources and provide comfort.
Energy accounting (Spoon Theory) is a critical self-management skill for preventing burnout.
A sensory diet proactively provides your brain with the inputs it needs to stay regulated.
Emotional literacy starts with the body: notice physical sensations first, then translate them into emotional language.
exercises: Design a foundational routine: Choose either your morning or evening and design a simple, 3–5 step routine you can practice consistently for the next week.
Your Spoons: Identify one high-cost activity (3+ spoons) and one recharging activity that gives you spoons back or costs zero spoons.
Emotional detective: Practice noticing physical sensations in your body. Write down 3–5 raw physical data points (e.g., chest tight, face hot, hands clenching) without trying to name the emotion yet.
homework: Energy Log: For at least three days this week, practice being an energy accountant. Create a log with columns: Activity | Predicted Spoon Cost (1–5) | Actual Spoon Cost (1–5) | Recharging Activity Used?

My Sensory Toolkit: Create categories for At Home, At Work/School, and In Public. For each category, list 2–3 specific items or actions you can use to regulate yourself. Choose one strategy and intentionally use it this week.
Foundational Routine Tracking: Note each day that you successfully complete your routine. How does it feel? What surprised you?

modules.title: Module 3 • Decoding Social Interactions
modules.overview: Having established a foundation of self-regulation, we now turn our attention outward to one of the most complex and energy-intensive aspects of daily life: social interaction. For many autistic people, the social world can feel like a game where everyone else intuitively knows the rules. Social interaction is not random—it is a system based on patterns. For a mind that excels at identifying patterns, this is a powerful reframe. Instead of trying to 'feel' your way through a conversation, you can learn to observe and analyze it. Most casual conversations follow a predictable, four-part structure: Initiation & Greetings, Small Talk as Data Exchange, Exchanging Information, and Ending a Conversation. Understanding this architecture allows you to know where you are in an interaction and what is expected next. Small talk is not pointless chatter—it's a low-stakes data-gathering process to establish connection and search for common ground. A simple formula is Observation + Question. Your autistic strength in observation is your greatest asset. Become a 'social detective' by observing from a distance, watching TV with a purpose, and formulating hypotheses about social rules. Social anxiety can be managed with CBT by challenging catastrophic thoughts. Ask: What is the evidence? What's a different way of looking at this? What can I do to prepare?
takeaways: Social interaction is a system of patterns, not a mystery. Your pattern-recognition skills are your greatest asset.
Conversations follow a predictable architecture: Initiation, Small Talk, Information Exchange, and Ending.
Small talk is data exchange—use the Observation + Question formula.
Being a social detective turns passive observation into active, structured learning.
exercises: Your Exit Line: Choose one exit line from the examples that feels comfortable for you. Write it down and commit it to memory.

Observation Log: Watch a 5–10 minute scene of a television show where people are having a casual conversation. Identify the parts: initiation, small talk topic, transition to deeper topic, and how it ended.
Develop a Small Talk Script: Choose one specific, common situation where you often need to make small talk. Create a simple, 3-step script: The Opener, The Follow-up, and The Gentle Exit.
homework: Observation Log: Watch a TV scene and document the conversational architecture, turn-taking patterns, and one 'unwritten rule' you observed.
Small Talk Script: Write down your 3-step script for a common situation and rehearse it.
Anxiety Log: If you experience social anxiety this week, apply the S-T-E-S-B model. Document the cycle and challenge the automatic thought with one realistic alternative perspective.

modules.title: Module 4 • A Practical Guide to Theory of Mind
modules.overview: After learning to decode the structure of conversations, we now tackle an even more complex challenge: understanding the hidden layer of human interaction. This module is about learning to infer what other people might be thinking and feeling—Theory of Mind or perspective-taking. Theory of Mind is not a deficit in empathy or character. It is a difference in cognitive processing. You can learn this skill through conscious, analytical effort—like learning a second language by studying the rules. You cannot read minds, but you can make educated guesses based on evidence. To infer what someone might be thinking or feeling, gather clues: Context (the situation), Tone of Voice (prosody), and Body Language. Synthesize all three clues to form your hypothesis. Figurative language can feel like a bug in the system for autistic brains wired for precision. Idioms must be memorized like vocabulary. Sarcasm is detected through a mismatch between words and context or tone. The master skill is asking for clarification politely and confidently. This is not a sign of failure; it is a sign of a careful and precise communicator. Build a Social 'Case Law' Library: systematically record and analyze social interactions. Document the Situation, Interaction, Outcome, and most importantly, the Rule (precedent) you learned.
takeaways: Theory of Mind is a learnable cognitive skill, not an unfixable flaw.
Gather three types of clues: Context, Tone of Voice, and Body Language. Synthesize them to form hypotheses.
Asking for clarification is a powerful and intelligent strategy, not a failure.
A Social Case Law Library turns confusing past events into valuable, reusable knowledge.
exercises: Practice a Clarification Phrase: Choose one clarification phrase that feels comfortable. Say it out loud three times and commit it to memory.

Perspective-Taking Practice: Watch a 2–3 minute scene from a movie or TV show. Hypothesize what each character is thinking and feeling, and identify the specific clues that led you to this hypothesis.
Decoding Practice: Identify one instance of figurative language or sarcasm you encountered. Analyze the clues that helped you decode it (or that you missed).
homework: Perspective-Taking Practice: Watch a scene and document your hypotheses about what characters are thinking and feeling, including the specific clues that led to your conclusions.
Clarification Practice: Find one low-stakes opportunity to practice asking for clarification. Document how it felt and what the outcome was.

Add to Your Case Law Library: Create the first entry in your Social Case Law Library. Document a recent interaction using the four-part structure: Situation, Interaction, Outcome, and Rule (precedent).

modules.title: Module 5 • Mastering Flexibility: Navigating Change and Uncertainty
modules.overview: Having built systems for internal regulation and social navigation, we now confront one of the greatest challenges for the autistic mind: change. The world is in a constant state of flux, and this unpredictability can be a major source of anxiety and distress. An unexpected change shatters your brain's predictive map. Your brain is forced to build a completely new map from scratch in real-time, an intensely energy-consuming process. The feeling of panic or shutdown that follows is not an overreaction; it is a logical response to a systemic crash. Black-and-white thinking leaves no room for error or nuance. Continuum Thinking places situations on a spectrum from 0 to 100, right-sizing problems so small disruptions don't have the power to ruin entire experiences. The 'Change Plan' is a proactive, four-step strategy: Information Gathering, Breaking the Change into Small Steps, Visualizing the New Routine, and Planning for Points of Uncertainty with If-Then Plans. For unexpected problems, use a 3-step emergency protocol: Pause & Regulate (calm your nervous system), Identify the Core Problem (isolate the concrete issue), and Choose One Next Action (break paralysis with a single small step).
takeaways: Change feels catastrophic because it shatters your brain's predictive map. This is a neurological reality, not an overreaction.
Continuum Thinking right-sizes problems by placing them on a 0–100 spectrum instead of binary success/failure.
The Change Plan reduces uncertainty by gathering information, breaking changes into steps, and creating If-Then plans.
The 3-step emergency protocol breaks paralysis: Pause & Regulate, Identify Core Problem, Choose One Next Action.
exercises: Place it on the Scale: Think of a recent minor setback. What was your initial black-and-white thought? Now rate it on a scale of 0 to 100. Where does it realistically fall?
Create a Change Plan: Choose a small, predictable change coming up. Apply the 4-step strategy: Information Gathering, Breaking into Steps, Visualizing New Routine, and creating one If-Then Plan.
Practice the Problem-Solving Model: The next time a small, unexpected problem occurs, consciously apply the 3-step emergency protocol and document the process.
homework: Challenge a Black-and-White Thought: Identify one instance of black-and-white thinking this week. Use the Continuum to rate it 0–100. Reflect on how reframing changed your feelings.
Create a Change Plan: Document all four steps of the Change Plan strategy for an upcoming predictable change in your notebook.
Practice the Problem-Solving Model: Apply the 3-step emergency protocol to a small, unexpected problem. Document how the structured approach helped you feel less overwhelmed.

modules.title: Module 6 • Integrating Special Interests & Executive Function
modules.overview: This module focuses on two deeply interconnected aspects: the immense power of your special interests and the unique challenges of executive functioning. We'll explore how to leverage your passions not just for joy, but as a powerful tool for motivation and regulation. Your special interest is a superpower: it's a source of joy and expertise, a powerful regulation tool that induces flow state, and a source of intrinsic motivation. Honoring and making time for your special interests is a fundamental act of self-care. Executive function challenges for autistic individuals often look different from ADHD. The difficulty is often not distraction, but inertia and rigidity. Autistic inertia is the profound difficulty in starting (or stopping) a task, often caused by overwhelm from bottom-up processing or a need for a perfect plan. Rigid sequencing is the feeling that tasks must be done in a specific order. The thought of starting with Step 3 when Step 1 isn't perfectly complete can feel deeply wrong, even if it would be more efficient. The 'First, Then' Method (Premack Principle) links a non-preferred task to a preferred one, using your special interest as an immediate reward. The formula: First, you do what you need to do. Then, you get to do what you want to do. The Chunking and Focusing Method combats overwhelm: Chunk the task into a complete list, then Focus on One Chunk Only by covering the list and working on just the first step. This honors your need for a complete plan while protecting you from overwhelm.
takeaways: Special interests are superpowers: sources of joy, regulation, and motivation. They are fundamental to autistic well-being.
Autistic inertia and rigid sequencing are common executive function challenges that require specific strategies.
The 'First, Then' Method uses your special interest as immediate, guaranteed motivation.
Chunking and Focusing honors your need for a complete plan while protecting you from overwhelm.
exercises: Interest-Based Motivation: Practice using the 'First, Then' method to complete one non-preferred task. Write down your statement with defined times for both activities.
Practice Chunking: Choose one large task that feels overwhelming. Create a master list of all steps, then use the Focus method—write only the first step on a sticky note and complete it.
Identify Your Inertia: Pay attention to a moment when you felt 'stuck' or unable to start a task. Analyze the cause: was it overwhelm, need for perfect plan, or rigid sequencing?
homework: Interest-Based Motivation: Use the 'First, Then' method this week. Document the task, reward, terms, and reflect on whether it made starting easier.
Practice Chunking: Create a master list for an overwhelming project. Use the Focus method for at least three consecutive chunks. Document the experience.
Executive Function Log: Document a moment of autistic inertia. Describe the situation, analyze the cause, and brainstorm one strategy you could try next time.

modules.title: Module 7 • Charting Your Own Path: Synthesis and Self-Advocacy
modules.overview: Welcome to the final module. You have dedicated significant time and energy to understanding your brain, learning new skills, and building practical strategies. This is a huge accomplishment. This last chapter is about synthesis and sustainability. Review your personal toolkit: not every tool will be equally useful. Identify the top 5 strategies that have been most helpful or resonant for you. These are your go-to supports for everyday challenges and moments of high stress. A Personal User Manual is a proactive tool for self-advocacy. It's a short, clear document that explains your communication style, strengths, and support needs. This is not a list of excuses; it is a guide to effective collaboration. Your Regulation Plan should have three zones: Green Zone (proactive prevention—foundational routines, downtime, sensory strategies), Yellow Zone (early intervention—identify warning signs and de-escalation strategies), and Red Zone (post-setback recovery—safety and recovery plan). Planning for setbacks (meltdowns, shutdowns, burnout) is not a sign of failure; it is a crucial part of a sustainable well-being plan. Having a plan ready means you don't have to invent a solution when you're already in crisis. Moving forward with autistic pride involves recognizing the value of your unique mind. Seek out the autistic community for validation and understanding. You are the expert on your own experience—chart your course accordingly.
takeaways: Review and consolidate your top 5 strategies into a personalized toolkit.
A Personal User Manual empowers you to define the terms of your interactions and reduce misunderstandings.
A three-zone Regulation Plan (Green, Yellow, Red) provides structure for prevention, early intervention, and recovery.
Autistic pride is about recognizing the value of your unique mind and embracing it as a core part of your identity.
exercises: Identify Your Top 5: Look back at all the strategies from the program. Write down the top 5 that have been most helpful or resonant for you.
Draft Your Personal User Manual: Write a first draft with at least one clear statement for Communication Style, Strengths, How to Work Best With Me, and Signs of Overload.
Develop Your Regulation Plan: Create your three-zone plan. List 3 proactive strategies (Green), 3 warning signs and 3 de-escalation strategies (Yellow), and 3 essential needs for recovery (Red).
homework: Draft Your Personal User Manual: Complete a first draft for a specific context (work, relationship, or general guide). Write one point for each section.
Develop Your Regulation Plan: Document all three zones in your notebook. Keep this plan accessible, perhaps as a note on your phone.
Commitment to Self-Advocacy: Identify one small, low-risk opportunity to advocate for one of your needs this week. Plan it, do it, and reflect on the experience.

aiSupport.systemPrompt: Help the user apply one concrete module step at a time. Do not diagnose. Escalate urgent safety concerns to emergency care.
